items.title: Alphonse Picou Interview, 1958-04-04
items.q: The Butcher? The Butcher cut it down? Didn't he ramble? Didn't he ramble? Uh-huh. That's one of them.

ctx.x: How much time did it usually take for the musicians to learn those tunes? If you had a new tune to put in, did they have to rehearse it very much? That depends. Uh-huh. I mean the blues were fast, all blues tunes were fast. But some of the more complicated things, you know, there were a lot of tunes that, uh, that were played in jazz later, but originally were played, uh, by, by, uh, regular bands, you know, brass bands. Yeah. Uh, which weren't jazz yet, you know? Uh, can you remember when any of those things…
The Butcher? The Butcher cut it down? Didn't he ramble? Didn't he ramble? Uh-huh. That's one of them. Didn't he ramble? Do you remember Muscat ramble? Oh, what's kept-
I mean, before, before the, did the bands always play Muscat ramble?

items.title: Alphonse Picou Interview, 1958-04-04
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] Yeah. George Bacchia. Yeah. George Bacchia. Yes. Lorenzo Tio and George Bacchia. We were the only three clarinet players in your league. [INTERVIEWEE] You know? Yeah.

ctx.x: Yeah. Yeah. But I was one of the leader. You know? Sure. That led them to that. Yeah. True jazz. Did you have any connection, any friendly connection or anything with some of the other clarinet players in those times like Lorenzo and I was playing with the jazz?
Yeah. George Bacchia. Yeah. George Bacchia. Yes. Lorenzo Tio and George Bacchia. We were the only three clarinet players in your league.
